newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss see EU negotiations reaching decisive stage.
newsitem.headline: Swiss see EU negotiations reaching decisive stage.

text.p: Switzerland gave negotiators fresh instructions on Wednesday for talks on boosting economic ties with the European Union and said it hoped soon to resolve the thorniest issue -- bilateral air and road links.

"The Federal Council (cabinet) believes talks have entered the decisive final phase," the seven-member executive said in a statement after meeting behind closed doors, adding both sides had to compromise to strike an acceptable deal.

"It has the firm desire to conclude bilateral talks quickly. To this end the Federal Council had determined certain elements on the basis of its discussions so that negotiations can continue," it said without elaborating.

This apparently referred to Berne's position on road fees it would charge for heavy trucks to roll through the country, a key sticking point in talks with Brussels over a transport accord. Officials declined to reveal any details.
"There are some things that cannot be negotiated in public," Transport Minister Moritz Leuenberger told reporters.

The transport pact is one of six issues in the package of deals designed to bind the Swiss economy more closely with that of the 15-member EU. Four have already been settled, and a fifth on the free movement of people is close to an agreement.

Berne and Brussels have already agreed the broad outline of a transport accord that would settle how much trucks should pay to transit Switzerland and the EU's demand for access for its 40-tonne trucks to Swiss industrial and commercial centres.
Switzerland currently bans trucks weighing more than 28 tonnes, and wants to use road fees to encourage trucks to make trips on railway cars rather than by road.

Unconfirmed Swiss media reports say Berne is prepared to cut its demand for "Alpine transit fees" to 450 Swiss francs ($307) per truck. That is below its previous demand for 600 francs, but above Brussels' last offer of 340.

Swiss environmentalists have vowed to force a referendum over any deal that charges trucks combined fees of less than 600 francs, arguing this amount would put nine out of 10 trucks on the rails and help limit environmental damage.
Talks between the Swiss government and Brussels began early in 1995,

Apart from transport -- which includes civil aviation -- and free movement of people the other four issues in the negotiations are agriculture, technical barriers to trade, government procurement and research and development.

The Swiss coalition government, which includes mainstream parties from right to left, favours joining the EU eventually but resistance persists among traditional-minded people, especially in the German-speaking part of the country.

In a referendum in 1992, Swiss voters rejected although by a narrow margin a proposal to join the European Economic Area, which linked the then seven-nation European Free Trade Association (EFTA) with the then European Community.
Since then, three of Switzerland's EFTA partners -- Finland, Sweden and its neighbour Austria -- have switched to the EU.

It was the refusal of the Swiss voters, many of whom said they feared loss of sovereignty and undermining of the country's political neutrality, to approve EEA membership that made the separate negotiations with Brussels necessary.
